subject: Climate & Environment
title: Buildings and Emissions
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Buildings and Emissions.

hook.text: Buildings are responsible for nearly 40% of global CO₂ emissions. Most people have no idea.

buildup.text: Heating, cooling, lighting, and cooking in buildings consume enormous amounts of energy.

discovery.text: Cement and steel production for construction adds billions more tons of embodied carbon.

twist.text: Most buildings standing in 2050 have already been built. Retrofitting them is essential.

climax.text: New building codes requiring efficiency and electrification could halve building emissions by 2050.

punchline.text: Every building you pass is a climate machine — mostly inefficient.

quiz.question: What share of global CO₂ emissions come from buildings?

details.summary: Buildings account for nearly 40 percent of global energy-related CO2 emissions through heating, cooling, lighting, and construction materials. Reducing building emissions requires both improving energy efficiency in existing structures and constructing new buildings to near-zero energy standards.
details.whyItMatters: With building stock growing rapidly in developing nations, locking in efficient design now prevents decades of excess emissions. Buildings are a top priority for urban decarbonization.
takeaways: Buildings produce nearly 40 percent of energy-related CO2
Heating and cooling dominate building energy consumption
New construction standards can cut emissions dramatically

faq.question: What is embodied carbon in buildings?
faq.answer: Embodied carbon is the CO2 emitted during manufacturing, transporting, and assembling building materials like steel, concrete, and glass. It can account for half of a building's lifetime emissions, especially in energy-efficient structures where operational emissions are low.

faq.question: Which building systems use the most energy?
faq.answer: Heating and cooling typically account for 40 to 60 percent of building energy use. Lighting and appliances follow. In hot climates, air conditioning dominates. In cold climates, space heating does. Water heating is significant everywhere.
